quote: The frequentist says, “No. Saying ‘probability 0.5’ means that the coin has an inherent propensity to come up heads as often as tails, so that if we flipped the coin infinitely many times, the ratio of heads to tails would approach 1:1. But we know that the coin is biased, so it can have any probability of coming up heads except 0.5.”
content: The speaker the essay calls a frequentist is holding two different theories at once and neither of them says what the essay needs. “Inherent propensity” is the propensity interpretation (Popper (1959)), a single-case objectivist view; “if we flipped infinitely many times” is the frequency interpretation (von Mises), on which the probability of this flip is undefined, not “anything but 0.5,” because a single event is not a collective. A frequentist statistician, which is the third thing the word can mean, would have no difficulty betting at even odds on the flip, since the practical methodology makes no claim about the flip’s probability at all. Gillies’s Philosophical Theories of Probability (2000, a book with no DOI) sorts these out in its first chapter. The essay’s dialogue works because the opponent has been assembled from the weakest parts of three positions; the actual objectivist reply is that “the coin is biased, and I don’t know which way, so my credence is 0.5” is a statement about the objective bias, which the Bayesian’s credence is tracking and which exists whether or not anyone tracks it.

This is Jaynes’s metaphysics stated as a result, and it is not the majority view in philosophy of probability or in physics. Lewis’s Principal Principle (“A Subjectivist’s Guide to Objective Chance,” 1980, a book chapter with no DOI) argues that even a thoroughgoing subjectivist needs objective chance to explain why a credence of 0.5 is the right one to have about a fair coin and 0.7 about a coin known to be 70/30; the credence is rational because it tracks something. In physics, radioactive decay and quantum measurement are chancy on the Copenhagen and objective-collapse readings and on the Everett reading the status of the Born probabilities is the unsolved problem that Opus’s annotation on Many Worlds records, so the book is asserting in this essay a conclusion that its own later argument does not secure. Even in deterministic settings there are objectivist accounts of the statistical-mechanical probabilities (Loewer (2001)) on which the probability that the egg reforms is a fact about the world’s dynamics and initial conditions rather than about anyone’s ignorance. The coin is not the test case: a coin flip is deterministic and everyone agrees the 0.5 is epistemic. The test cases are decay and measurement, and the essay does not mention them.

quote: What is the probability that she has two boys? If you assume that the prior probability of a child’s being a boy is 1/2, then the probability that she has two boys, on the information given, is 1/3.
content: The calculation is correct for the protocol the essay specifies (you ask a yes/no question and she answers truthfully), and the essay is careful to specify it. But the diagnosis of why the problem feels paradoxical is not the one the literature gives. The Boy or Girl paradox turns on the unstated sampling protocol by which the information reached you: if the mathematician had instead volunteered “one of my children is a boy” after picking a child at random and reporting its sex, the answer is 1/2, and Gardner, who popularized the problem in 1959, retracted his original 1/3 for that reason. Bar-Hillel & Falk (1982) showed that the same is true of the essay’s card version and of Monty Hall: the likelihood of the report, not the content of the report, is what conditioning must use, and the paradox is the feeling that “at least one is a boy” carries the same information regardless of how one came to know it. That is a lesson about likelihoods of observation processes, and it is entirely available to someone who thinks probabilities are in the world. The essay’s moral, that the paradox comes from “thinking that the probabilities must be properties of the cards themselves,” misidentifies which mistake the puzzle is exploiting: a propensity theorist who conditions on the report correctly gets 1/3 too.

quote: But maybe a robot with extra-sensitive eyes and a good grasp of physics, watching the autoflipper prepare to flip, could predict the coin’s fall in advance—not with certainty, but with 90% accuracy.
content: This thought experiment was run, and the essay is right about it. Diaconis, Holmes & Montgomery (2007) built a mechanical coin flipper that produces the same outcome every time from the same initial conditions, and showed by analysis of the dynamics that a natural human flip lands on the side that started facing up about 51% of the time, a bias later confirmed in a preregistered study of over 350,000 flips (Bartoš et al., 2023). The coin has no probability in it; the outcome is fixed by the launch, and an observer who measures the launch well enough predicts it. This is the strongest empirical support for the essay’s thesis about coins, and the essay supplies it as a hypothetical. It does not extend to the cases that matter for the “no real probability” claim, since a decay event has no launch conditions to measure on any interpretation but Bohm’s, but for the example the essay chose, the robot exists and it wins.
